Now I get why Vanilla PINNs are so brittle for forward problems! And why old
school numericists frown at it. They are essentially a half-baked Weighted
Residuals Method (that happens to use Autodiff in a very clever way).

Why do I say that? It’s a long history...

![A physics-informed neural network (PINN) predicting a flow field governed by the Navier–Stokes equations. Image: [Amirhossein Arzani](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Physics-informed_nerural_networks_Navier-Stokes.png), [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), via Wikimedia Commons.](figures/pinns-navier-stokes.png){fig-alt="PINN predicting a Navier–Stokes flow field"}

I was studying the Finite Element Method (FEM), and to understand the
nomenclature, I had to go back to the father of *ALL* numerical simulation
methods: the *Weighted Residuals Method* (WRM).

In this method, we have a differential operator ($\mathcal{P}$), a forcing
function ($f$), a "trial function" ($u$, a candidate solution we pass to the
operator to check the error), and a "test function" ($v$, which weights how much
we care about the solution deviating from the true field over the domain). We
need the test function because finding a perfectly matched solution over all of
the domain for an arbitrary PDE would require infinite degrees of freedom (and
therefore infinite compute and memory).

$$
  \int_{\Omega} v \left( \mathcal{P}u - f \right) \, d\Omega = 0 . 
$$

Back in the day, mathematicians used this to systematically verify "trials" at
solutions found via intuition or analytical methods — hence "trial function."
But they soon realized this same machinery could guide the development and
classify numerical methods.

Every numerical method is just a choice of how to build the trial function, the
test function, and how to solve the resulting optmization problem. (And yes,
there is always a hidden optimization problem. We just don't realize it because
many methods are designed to end up in closed-form optimization problem — but
when iterative solvers pop up, the optimization nature shows its face in any
method).

# This brings us to why PINNs struggle with forward problems.

If you choose your test function to be a Dirac delta over a fixed grid,
congratulations: you’ve built a "collocation method." The Dirac delta means: "I
want my solution to be exact at these specific coordinates." Sounds good, right?
But because this constraint is so strong, the solution can end up contorting
itself wildly between the points to satisfy it. This causes classic numerical
nightmares like checkerboard patterns and Runge phenomena.

To fix this, classical numericists use inductive bias, which means, to bias the
structure of the test and trial functions in a given direction that they know
that is coherent with the mathematical structure being represented in order to
constraint the space of possible solutions (hopefully to a unique solution).
Collocation methods (like FDM) bias the trial function using local stencils
to keep the solution stiff and well-behaved. The Finite Element Method (FEM)
goes even further: it throws away the Dirac delta entirely, using a smoother
test function (the "Hat" function) and a Weak Form to relax the constraints
and average out the error. The Finite Volume Method (FVM), bake the physics of
conservation itself in the method.

# So why is the Vanilla PINN half-baked?

Because it uses the most naive approach possible: a Dirac delta test function
over a random cloud of points, and a plain neural network (a standard MLP) as
the trial function. A plain neural network is a universal approximator with
zero inductive bias for this kind of task. And you try to satisfy strong,
point-wise constraints with a hyper-flexible, global rubber sheet. The result is
a terrible, non-convex optimization landscape, full of spurious local minima.

This has a charm that PINNs come as close to a "pure" WRM as possible by
leveraging Autodiff. But in doing so, they throw 50 years of numerical research
out the window.

Nonetheless, that elegant use of Autodiff inspired a ton of new methods (like
Variational PINNs and Neural Operators). So, despite being half-baked, PINNs
deserve a place in every numerical developer's heart!
